original_question: Let q be a power of a prime p, and let mn(q) be the maximum p-length of p-solvable subgroups of GL(n, q). Is it true that lim mn(q)/ log2 n = 1? İ. Güloğlu n→∞
target_in_paper: Problem 21.55 in the section "New Problems (21st issue, 2026)"
correct_elements: Your draft matches the paper's official problem almost verbatim: it uses the same parameters q and p with q a power of p, the same quantity m_n(q) defined via the maximum p-length of p-solvable subgroups of GL(n, q), and the same asymptotic question asking whether lim_{n->infty} m_n(q)/log_2 n = 1.
missing_details: It should make explicit that q is fixed while n tends to infinity.
It should spell out that GL(n, q) means the finite general linear group GL_n(F_q) over the field with q elements.
It should state explicitly that the maximum is taken over all p-solvable subgroups H <= GL_n(F_q).
It should define p-length as the standard p-length l_p(H) of a finite p-solvable group.
It should specify that n ranges over positive integers and that log_2 is the base-2 logarithm.
refined_question: For a fixed prime power q = p^f, let GL_n(F_q) be the general linear group over the field F_q, and define m_n(q) := max{ l_p(H) : H <= GL_n(F_q) and H is p-solvable }, where l_p(H) denotes the p-length of the finite p-solvable group H. Is it true that lim_{n->infty} m_n(q)/log_2(n) = 1?
justification: The draft is targeting the paper's Problem 21.55 exactly. The paper states only this asymptotic question and does not supply, in the nearby text, a sharper equivalent reformulation or additional hypotheses. So the most faithful refinement is to preserve the statement itself while unpacking the standard notation needed to make it fully stand-alone.
